topic: git object model as a Merkle DAG / content addressing
question: Explain in what precise sense a Git repository is a Merkle DAG rather than merely a hash chain. Which four object types participate, how does an edge get its 'address', and why is the resulting graph necessarily acyclic?
reference_answer: Git's four object types — blob, tree, commit and tag — are each stored under an object ID that is the cryptographic hash of the object's exact serialised content, i.e. content addressing (git-scm: 'All objects are named by the SHA-1 hash of their contents ... globally unique'). Objects embed the IDs of other objects: a commit names its root tree and parent commit(s) by hash; a tree names its blobs and sub-trees by hash; a tag names its target by hash. Because every edge is the hash of the target object, the links are authenticated Merkle links, forming a directed acyclic graph (a Merkle DAG), not a linear chain — a commit fans out to a whole tree of trees and blobs. It is acyclic because an object's ID is fixed by its content: you cannot make object A reference a not-yet-existing hash of B that in turn references A, since changing content produces a new hash and hence a new object rather than mutating the target in place.
answer_key_points: Four object types: blob, tree, commit, tag
Object ID = cryptographic hash of the object's serialised content (content addressing)
Edges are hashes of target objects (Merkle links), so links are authenticated
DAG, not a chain: commits fan out to trees which fan out to blobs/sub-trees
Acyclic because content determines the hash — you cannot embed a hash of an object that embeds you

topic: git SHA-1 to SHA-256 object-format transition
question: Git supports a SHA-256 object format. In a repository created for the transition, what do the config extensions objectFormat and compatObjectFormat do, what auxiliary data structure must a SHA-256 repository store alongside its packfile, and what is the current state of interoperability with SHA-1 repositories?
reference_answer: A transition-era repository uses core.repositoryFormatVersion = 1 with extensions.objectFormat = sha256 (the storage hash, which determines the 64-hex-digit object IDs) and extensions.compatObjectFormat = sha1 (a compatibility hash that must differ from objectFormat). To make objects addressable under both algorithms, a SHA-256 repository stores a bidirectional mapping between SHA-256 and SHA-1 object names alongside the packfile, so objects can be named by either their 40-hex SHA-1 or 64-hex SHA-256 IDs. SHA-1 remains the default object format, SHA-256 support is still marked experimental, and there is presently no general interoperability between SHA-256 and SHA-1 repositories — they cannot share work and old Git versions cannot read a SHA-256 repository. Git's BreakingChanges plan intends to eventually switch the default for new repositories to SHA-256 once ecosystem support is sufficient, but there is no plan to deprecate the SHA-1 object format.
answer_key_points: objectFormat = the storage hash (sha256 => 64-hex object IDs); default is sha1
compatObjectFormat = a compatibility hash, must differ from objectFormat, for format-1 interop testing
SHA-256 repos store a bidirectional SHA-256<->SHA-1 name mapping beside the packfile
Objects can be named by 40-hex SHA-1 or 64-hex SHA-256 IDs
No interoperability today; SHA-256 support is experimental; old Git cannot read SHA-256 repos
Planned default switch to SHA-256 later; SHA-1 format not being deprecated

topic: hardened SHA-1 (sha1dc) collision detection in Git
question: Given that SHA-1 has been practically broken (SHAttered, 2017), why can Git still use SHA-1-named objects relatively safely today? Name the specific mechanism modern Git builds employ and describe what it actually detects.
reference_answer: Modern Git builds do not use plain SHA-1; they use a hardened SHA-1 implementation, sha1dc (SHA-1 collision detection, by Stevens and Shumow), as the default hash. sha1dc computes the ordinary SHA-1 digest but simultaneously runs a detection algorithm that watches for the specific disturbance-vector / message-block patterns characteristic of a SHA-1 collision attack (the identical-prefix collision technique used by SHAttered). If such a pattern is detected it aborts rather than emitting a digest, so a crafted colliding object is rejected. This mitigates the known collision constructions cheaply, but it is a stop-gap: it does not make SHA-1 collision-resistant against future novel attacks, which is why Git is separately building out the SHA-256 object format. sha1dc is an implementation-level defence and is complementary to, not a substitute for, the architectural move to SHA-256.
answer_key_points: Git uses hardened SHA-1 = sha1dc (collision-detecting SHA-1), not plain SHA-1, by default
sha1dc detects the disturbance-vector/message-block signatures of known SHA-1 collision attacks
It aborts instead of returning a digest when an attack pattern is seen, rejecting crafted colliding objects
Mitigates SHAttered-style identical-prefix collisions cheaply
It is a stop-gap; does not restore general collision resistance — hence the parallel SHA-256 transition

topic: signed commits and the absence of trusted time
question: A colleague argues that GPG- or SSH-signed Git commits (git commit -S) already prove exactly when a commit was made and therefore give a complete provenance trail. Identify the precise guarantee a signed commit provides, the field that makes the 'when' claim untrustworthy, and why an external timestamp is still needed.
reference_answer: A signed commit binds a specific signing key to the exact hashed commit payload: the signature (stored in the gpgsig header) covers the commit object — its tree, parent(s), author/committer identities and message — so any alteration invalidates it, verifiable with git verify-commit or git log --show-signature. That is an authenticity/integrity guarantee ('this key endorsed this content'), not a trusted-time guarantee. The commit's author and committer date fields are simply attacker-controllable strings set by the client; nothing in the signature attests that the commit really existed at that moment, and back- or forward-dating is trivial. To obtain a trustworthy 'existed no later than T' you need an external anchor — e.g. an OpenTimestamps proof anchoring the commit hash to a Bitcoin block, or a transparency-log inclusion — because only a third party with independent time (a blockchain, a log, a timestamping authority) can bound existence in time.
answer_key_points: Signed commit = key binds to the hashed commit object (tree, parents, identities, message) via the gpgsig header
Provides authenticity/integrity, verifiable with git verify-commit / git log --show-signature
The author/committer date fields are client-set and attacker-controllable — not attested by the signature
Signatures give no trusted time; back-/forward-dating is trivial
A trusted 'existed before T' needs an external anchor (OpenTimestamps/blockchain or a transparency log)

question: git notes let you attach metadata to an existing commit without changing that commit's hash. Explain how notes are stored, why attaching a note leaves the annotated commit's object ID unchanged, and what this implies for using notes to carry provenance data such as a reference to an external timestamp proof.
reference_answer: A git note is itself a blob (extra information supplementing an object, usually a commit), stored not inside the target commit but in a separate notes ref — by default refs/notes/commits — whose tree maps target object names (paths) to the note blobs. Because the note lives in an independent ref rather than in the commit object, the annotated commit's serialised content, and therefore its object ID, is unchanged; this is precisely why notes can be added, edited or removed after the fact and can annotate immutable, even signed, commits. The trade-off is that notes are not covered by a signature over the original commit: the note ref has its own separate Git history (its own hash chain) that can itself be signed or protected, but a signature on the commit does not vouch for its notes. So notes are a good place to record provenance pointers — e.g. the ID or hash of an OpenTimestamps .ots proof for the commit — provided you separately protect the notes ref, since the annotation's integrity is independent of the commit's.
answer_key_points: A note is a blob stored in a separate notes ref (default refs/notes/commits), keyed by target object name
The commit object is not modified, so its object ID stays the same — hence notes can annotate immutable/signed commits
Notes are mutable after the fact (add/edit/remove) precisely because they are external to the commit
A signature over the commit does NOT cover its notes; the notes ref has its own hash chain
Good for carrying provenance pointers (e.g. an .ots proof ID) but the notes ref must be protected/signed separately

topic: OpenTimestamps aggregation, calendar servers and Bitcoin anchoring
question: OpenTimestamps claims it can timestamp an unlimited number of documents with a single Bitcoin transaction. Explain the aggregation mechanism, the role of calendar servers and their trust model, and describe precisely how the commitment reaches Bitcoin — in particular whether OpenTimestamps uses OP_RETURN or relies only on the block's transaction Merkle root.
reference_answer: Clients submit only the hash of a document to a calendar server. The calendar aggregates every request received in the same short interval (about one second) into a single Merkle tree, whose tip (root) is one 32-byte digest committing to all those documents at once; each client gets back a proof consisting of the operations (sibling hashes) climbing from its document hash to that tip — which is why one Bitcoin transaction can anchor unlimited documents. The calendar's job is a trust compromise: it must ensure every aggregated tip is eventually anchored on Bitcoin and keep the completed proofs available, but it need not be trusted for correctness because the finished proof verifies entirely against the blockchain. As for reaching Bitcoin: per Peter Todd, the calendar creates a Bitcoin transaction that commits to that single 32-byte tip, and the currently deployed calendar servers embed the digest directly in an OP_RETURN output. That transaction is then itself a leaf of the block's transaction Merkle tree, so the block header's merkleroot is the ultimate commitment — but the specific mechanism to get the digest into the block today is OP_RETURN, not (yet) a subtler tx-structure commitment (an alternative Poelstra scheme exists as a 2017 PR but is not in the standard protocol).
answer_key_points: Clients send only a document hash; requests in a ~1-second interval are aggregated into one Merkle tree
The tree tip is a single 32-byte digest; each client's proof is the sibling-hash path from its hash to the tip
One Bitcoin transaction thus anchors an unlimited number of documents
Calendars must anchor tips and keep proofs available, but need not be trusted — proofs verify against the blockchain
Deployed calendars embed the tip directly in an OP_RETURN output (per Peter Todd)
The block header's transaction merkleroot is the ultimate commitment; the alternative non-OP_RETURN scheme is not in the standard protocol

topic: git-mark: anchoring git commits to a blockchain
question: Describe the git-mark tool's model for making a Git repository's history tamper-evident against a public ledger. What is the role of the 'genesis' transaction, what does invoking the mark do, and how does this differ in guarantee from Git's internal hash chain plus signed commits?
reference_answer: git-mark (invoked as `git mark`, distributed via npm) anchors Git commits onto a supporting blockchain (Bitmark, framed as Bitcoin-like) to create an auditable, tamper-proof record. On first use you bind the repository to a genesis unspent transaction with `git mark --genesis txid:output`; this fixes the starting point of a per-repository chain of mark transactions. Each subsequent `git mark` advances that chain by creating a new blockchain transaction that commits to the current Git HEAD commit hash plus metadata, so once the block confirms, that commit state is anchored under public consensus and cannot be rewritten without contradicting the ledger. The difference in guarantee is the external anchor: Git's own hash chain plus signed commits only prove internal integrity and author endorsement — they are tamper-evident merely relative to another copy of the repo, and a force-push can rewrite history undetectably if no external reference exists. Anchoring the HEAD hash to a blockchain moves the guarantee from 'tamper-evident within Git' to 'tamper-evident against a global, time-ordered consensus ledger', giving proof of existence and state at a confirmed block time.
answer_key_points: git-mark (`git mark`, via npm) anchors commit hashes to a supporting blockchain (Bitmark)
`git mark --genesis txid:output` binds the repo to a genesis unspent transaction, starting a mark chain
Each `git mark` creates a new tx committing to the current HEAD commit hash + metadata; block confirmation anchors it
Git's hash chain + signed commits give only internal integrity/authenticity, tamper-evident relative to another copy
A force-push can rewrite history undetectably without an external reference; the blockchain anchor removes that gap
Result: proof of existence/state against a global consensus ledger, not just within Git

topic: OpenTimestamps git integration via a GPG wrapper
question: OpenTimestamps ships a Git integration that timestamps PGP-signed commits. Describe the wrapper mechanism it uses to hook into git commit -S, the git config setting that activates it, and explain the specific provenance problem this solves that an ordinary signed commit does not.
reference_answer: The OpenTimestamps client hooks into Git by wrapping the GPG program that Git invokes when signing. It provides an ots-git-gpg-wrapper (with a shell entry point ots-git-gpg-wrapper.sh); you activate it with `git config --global gpg.program <path to ots-git-gpg-wrapper.sh>`. Thereafter `git commit -S` calls the wrapper instead of GPG directly: the wrapper produces the normal commit signature via GPG and additionally creates an OpenTimestamps proof that anchors the commit/signature to Bitcoin through the calendar servers (with options such as --wait to block until the timestamp is upgraded). The problem this solves is temporal: an ordinary signed commit only proves 'this key signed this content', with no trustworthy time. If the signing key is later revoked, expired or compromised, a plain signature becomes ambiguous — you cannot tell whether it was made while the key was still valid. The Bitcoin-anchored timestamp proves the signature existed before a specific block time, i.e. before the revocation, letting verifiers still trust signatures that pre-date a key's compromise.
answer_key_points: Integration wraps the GPG program Git calls: ots-git-gpg-wrapper (ots-git-gpg-wrapper.sh)
Activated via `git config gpg.program <wrapper>` (typically --global)
On `git commit -S` the wrapper both produces the GPG signature and creates an OTS proof anchoring to Bitcoin via calendars
A plain signed commit proves only 'key signed content', with no trustworthy time
Anchoring proves the signature existed before a given block time — crucial once a key is revoked/expired/compromised
Lets verifiers still trust signatures that pre-date a key's compromise

topic: RFC 6962 Merkle tree domain separation (0x00 / 0x01 prefixes)
question: In RFC 6962 (Certificate Transparency), the Merkle Tree Hash prepends a single byte before hashing at each node: 0x00 for leaves and 0x01 for interior nodes. Give the exact leaf and interior-node hash definitions, and explain the security property this domain separation provides.
reference_answer: RFC 6962 builds a binary Merkle tree over an ordered list of entries using SHA-256. For a single-entry list the leaf hash is MTH({d[0]}) = SHA-256(0x00 || d[0]). For n > 1, letting k be the largest power of two strictly less than n, the interior node is MTH(D[n]) = SHA-256(0x01 || MTH(D[0:k]) || MTH(D[k:n])). The distinct prefix bytes 0x00 (leaf) and 0x01 (interior) implement domain separation: the input spaces of leaf hashes and interior-node hashes are made disjoint, so no leaf hash can ever equal an interior-node hash. This blocks second-preimage / tree-structure ambiguity attacks in which an adversary would present a leaf whose value coincides with the concatenation of two child hashes (or vice versa), thereby forging a different tree shape that hashes to the same root. Without the prefixes such a structural collision would be possible even though SHA-256 itself is collision-resistant.
answer_key_points: Interior (n>1, k = largest power of two < n): MTH = SHA-256(0x01 || MTH(D[0:k]) || MTH(D[k:n]))
0x00 vs 0x01 = domain separation making leaf and interior hash inputs disjoint
No leaf hash can collide with an interior-node hash
Prevents second-preimage / tree-reshaping attacks where a leaf value mimics a child-hash concatenation
Needed because such structural ambiguity would exist even with a collision-resistant SHA-256

topic: RFC 6962 inclusion vs consistency proofs, STH and Maximum Merge Delay
question: Distinguish a Merkle audit path (inclusion proof) from a Merkle consistency proof in an RFC 6962 transparency log: what does each one prove, what inputs does each need, what does a Signed Tree Head contain, and what is the Maximum Merge Delay?
reference_answer: An audit path (inclusion proof) proves that one specific leaf is present in a tree of a given size: given the leaf hash, the list of sibling hashes up to the root, and the root hash from a Signed Tree Head, the verifier recomputes the root and checks it matches — it proves membership of a single item. A consistency proof instead proves the append-only property between two tree states: given two STHs of sizes m <= n, it is the minimal set of node hashes needed to show the smaller tree of size m is a prefix of the larger tree of size n, i.e. that nothing was deleted or rewritten, only appended. A Signed Tree Head is the log's signed commitment to its current state, containing the tree size, the root (tree-head) hash, a timestamp and the log's signature (plus log-identifying metadata). The Maximum Merge Delay (MMD) is a log-declared time bound within which any accepted certificate must be incorporated into the tree and covered by a new STH; a client can therefore demand an inclusion proof against any STH dated after SCT-timestamp + MMD, and a log that fails to honour its MMD is treated as misbehaving.
answer_key_points: Inclusion/audit proof: sibling hashes from a leaf to the root; proves one leaf is in the tree of a given STH
Consistency proof: node hashes proving tree of size m is a prefix of tree of size n (m<=n) — append-only, nothing deleted/altered
Inclusion needs leaf hash + audit path + STH root; consistency needs two STH roots/sizes + consistency path
STH contains: tree size, root (tree-head) hash, timestamp, log signature (and log ID metadata)
MMD = log-declared max time to incorporate an accepted cert into the tree and cover it with an STH
Client verifies inclusion against an STH dated after SCT timestamp + MMD; failing MMD = misbehaviour

topic: Google Trillian personalities and tile-based logs
question: Google Trillian is a general-purpose verifiable-log backend. What is a Trillian 'personality' and what three kinds of responsibility does it own that the Trillian core deliberately does not? Separately, what is a 'tile' in tile-based transparency logs and what problem does tiling address?
reference_answer: Trillian core is a generic, storage-backed append-only Merkle tree that provides sequencing and inclusion/consistency proofs but no application semantics. A personality is the application layer built on top of that core for a specific kind of log (a CT log, a key-transparency log, a software-supply-chain log, etc.), and it owns three responsibilities the core intentionally omits: (1) admission criteria — deciding what may be logged (e.g. only valid X.509 certificates); (2) canonicalisation — mapping equivalent submissions to a canonical form so the core can de-duplicate; and (3) the external interface — the client-facing API, ACLs, rate-limiting and DoS protection, which it translates into core operations like QueueLeaf and GetInclusionProof. A tile, in tile-based logs, is a fixed-size subtree of Merkle nodes (a group of hashes) stored and served as one unit; tiling batches the tree's hashes so that storage, recomputation and proof-serving read a small number of tiles rather than walking individual nodes, greatly reducing per-request overhead and making the log cheap to serve and mirror.
answer_key_points: Trillian core = generic storage-backed append-only Merkle tree with inclusion/consistency proofs, no app semantics
A personality = the application layer for a specific log type on top of the core
Personality owns: (1) admission criteria (what may be logged)
(2) canonicalisation (equivalent submissions -> canonical form for de-duplication)
(3) external interface/API, ACLs, rate-limiting/DoS; maps to core ops like QueueLeaf/GetInclusionProof
A tile = a fixed-size subtree/group of Merkle hashes stored and served as one unit; tiling cuts storage/recompute/proof-serving overhead and eases mirroring

question: AluVM is the RISC virtual machine that runs RGB contract validation scripts. Describe its register file and explain the concrete mechanisms by which it guarantees deterministic, exception-free execution with no undefined behaviour. In particular, what happens to a destination register on an impossible operation, what is the role of the st0 register, and how is control flow made total (no invalid jumps or instructions)?
reference_answer: AluVM is a register-based (no random-access memory), purely functional RISC VM. Its integer arithmetic 'A' registers are organised as 8 blocks of 32 registers each, of widths 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256, 512 and 1024 bits; there are large 'R' registers reserved for cryptography (elliptic-curve/hashing) and a single block of 256 'S' string registers of up to 64 KiB each, plus control registers headed by the boolean status register st0. Exception-freedom comes from making every register nullable: any impossible, invalid or type-mismatched operation does not trap — it simply sets the destination register to a special undefined ('None') state, so there is always a representable result. Failures of flagged (checked) operations (e.g. checked-arithmetic overflow or a NaN float result) are signalled by setting st0 to false. Control flow is made total because the code is always zero-extended to 2^16 bytes, and the all-zero byte decodes to a valid opcode meaning 'set st0 to false and stop', so there are no invalid instructions and no out-of-range jumps; cycles and jumps are counted against a 2^16 limit to bound execution time.
answer_key_points: A-registers: 8 blocks of 32 registers, widths 8/16/32/64/128/256/512/1024 bits
S-registers: one block of 256 registers, up to 64 KiB each; R-registers reserved for cryptography
Every register can hold an undefined/None state; impossible ops set destination to undefined instead of trapping
st0 is the boolean status register; flagged operations set st0=false on overflow/NaN/failure
Code is zero-padded to 2^16 bytes; the zero opcode means 'set st0=false and stop' -> no invalid instructions/jumps
Cycles and jumps are counted with a 2^16 limit for bounded-time execution

question: LNPBP-1 defines the base cryptographic-commitment primitive used throughout RGB. Give the exact tweaked-key formula, and explain three specific design choices: why the message is authenticated with HMAC-SHA256 rather than a plain hash, what the HMAC key is, and why the standard deliberately uses no nonce.
reference_answer: LNPBP-1 commits to a message by tweaking a public key: T = Po + G * HMAC-SHA256(SHA256("LNPBP1") || SHA256(tag) || msg, S*), where Po is the chosen original key from the set, G is the secp256k1 generator, and the commitment is added to the whole keyset via S* — the 64-byte uncompressed serialization (x||y, with the 0x04 prefix stripped) of the sum S of all unique public keys controlling the output. HMAC-SHA256 is used instead of a plain hash to make arbitrary-length messages immune to length-extension attacks, and the HMAC key is S* — using the public-key sum both binds the commitment to those keys and injects entropy. The double-tagged prefix SHA256("LNPBP1") || SHA256(tag) is a BIP-340-style tagged-hash that prevents cross-protocol replay/reinterpretation. No nonce is added because the public key S already supplies enough entropy through the HMAC to defeat brute-force/dictionary attacks on short messages.
answer_key_points: T = Po + G * HMAC-SHA256(SHA256("LNPBP1") || SHA256(tag) || msg, S*)
Commits to the SUM of all unique keys in the output, not just one key
S* is the 64-byte uncompressed sum key (x||y, 0x04 prefix stripped) and serves as the HMAC key
HMAC-SHA256 chosen to prevent length-extension attacks on arbitrary-length messages
Double SHA256 tagged prefix prevents cross-protocol collision/replay
No nonce: the public-key sum already provides sufficient entropy

question: LNPBP-2 embeds an LNPBP-1 commitment deterministically into a Bitcoin output's scriptPubkey. Why does it commit to the sum of ALL public keys in the script, how does it deterministically decide which key carries the commitment across arbitrary script types, and what happens for a Taproot (P2TR) output? What extra data must be kept off-chain for verification?
reference_answer: LNPBP-2 requires that exactly one key of all keys present in the scriptPubkey/redeemScript/witnessScript carries the LNPBP-1 tweak, but the tweak commits to the SUM of all original (pre-tweak) public keys controlling the output; committing to the sum is what makes the commitment 'deterministically singular', i.e. provably free of an alternative message under the protocol. To find keys deterministically and implementation-independently, the script is parsed with Miniscript and all pk keys are collected; if a key-hash (pk_h) is encountered that cannot be resolved to a known key the procedure fails, which blocks a multiple-commitment attack via differing extra-transaction proofs. For a Taproot output the internal (intermediate) key is tweaked rather than the output key, because tweaking the output key would break its BIP-341 commitment to the script tree and make the output unspendable. Verification needs an off-chain extra-transaction proof (ETP): the original untweaked key/keyset plus script-reconstruction data (e.g. the untweaked redeemScript/witnessScript, or the Taproot merkle-root/taptweak), which is replayed to regenerate and byte-match the scriptPubkey.
answer_key_points: Exactly one key is tweaked, but it commits to the SUM of all original keys in the output -> deterministic singularity
Keys extracted deterministically via Miniscript parsing of the script
Procedure fails on an unresolvable pk_h to prevent multiple-commitment attacks
For P2TR the internal/intermediate key is tweaked, not the output key (else BIP-341 commitment breaks)
Verification requires an off-chain extra-transaction proof (ETP): original keys + script/taptweak reconstruction data

question: LNPBP-4 lets a single Bitcoin commitment carry messages from multiple independent protocols while proving uniqueness in zero knowledge. Describe how a message is placed into the commitment buffer, how empty slots are filled, and how the scheme proves both that a given protocol's commitment is present and that no second commitment under the same protocol exists.
reference_answer: LNPBP-4 allocates a buffer of N 32-byte slots with N much greater than the number of messages M (N is a 16-bit number, so the buffer is capped at ~2 MB). Each protocol has a unique 256-bit id, and its commitment is written into slot n = id mod N; because the position is a deterministic function of the protocol id, two commitments under the same protocol id would collide on the same slot and thus cannot both be present — which is the uniqueness guarantee. Remaining empty slots are filled with deterministic pseudo-random data: a BIP-340 tagged hash (tag "LNPBP4:entropy") of entropy_seed || j for slot index j. The whole buffer is then committed with LNPBP-1/2 using the tag "LNPBP4". A partial (per-message) reveal discloses the message, its protocol id and the full buffer, letting a verifier recompute slot n and match it — without learning the other messages. A full-disclosure reveal additionally provides entropy_seed so a verifier can regenerate every filler slot and confirm the buffer contains only the declared commitments and no hidden extra ones.
answer_key_points: Buffer of N 32-byte slots, N >> M, capped at ~2 MB (16-bit slot count)
Each protocol has a unique 256-bit id; commitment placed at slot n = id mod N
Same-protocol-id collision on the same slot is what guarantees per-protocol uniqueness
Empty slots filled with BIP-340 tagged hash (tag 'LNPBP4:entropy') of entropy_seed||j
Final buffer committed via LNPBP-1/2 with tag 'LNPBP4'
Partial reveal proves presence; full reveal (with entropy_seed) proves absence of other commitments

topic: Tapret vs Opret deterministic Bitcoin commitments
question: RGB anchors its MPC commitment into a Bitcoin transaction using one of two deterministic-bitcoin-commitment (DBC) schemes: Opret and Tapret. Contrast their exact on-chain form and byte sizes, and explain what the 1-byte nonce in a Tapret commitment is for.
reference_answer: Opret is the simple scheme: the 32-byte MPC commitment is placed in the first OP_RETURN output of the witness transaction as 'OP_RETURN OP_PUSHBYTES_32 <mpc::Commitment>', a 34-byte script that is visible on-chain. Tapret hides the commitment inside a Taproot script tree instead, giving a smaller/indistinguishable chain footprint and better privacy. The Tapret commitment is a fixed 64-byte tapscript leaf: 29 bytes of a fixed prefix (OP_RESERVED) followed by OP_RETURN, a 33-byte push holding the 32-byte MPC commitment plus a 1-byte nonce; this leaf is inserted as an unspendable script at the first level of the tree, shifting any existing scripts one level down. Because Taproot hashes branch pairs in lexicographic order, the commitment leaf may land on the left, forcing a larger uniqueness proof that reveals sibling branches. The 1-byte nonce exists so the prover can 'mine' the leaf hash until it is greater than the rest of the tree and therefore sits on the right-hand side, which keeps the uniqueness/inclusion proof minimal and avoids revealing private sibling scripts.
answer_key_points: Opret: 32-byte commitment in first OP_RETURN output; script = OP_RETURN OP_PUSHBYTES_32 <commit>, 34 bytes, on-chain visible
Tapret: commitment hidden in Taproot script tree for smaller footprint/better privacy
Tapret leaf is exactly 64 bytes: 29-byte fixed prefix + OP_RETURN + 33-byte push (32-byte MPC commitment + 1-byte nonce)
Tapret leaf inserted as unspendable script, shifting existing scripts down a level
Lexicographic branch ordering means left-placement needs a larger uniqueness proof
The 1-byte nonce is 'mined' so the leaf hash sorts to the right side, minimising the proof

question: Single-use-seals are the anti-double-spend primitive underpinning RGB. State the abstract operations a single-use-seal implementation must provide, give the precise security property a secure implementation must satisfy, and explain how Bitcoin is used to realise a trust-minimised seal.
reference_answer: A single-use-seal is a unique object that can be 'closed' over a message exactly once. An implementation must support Close(l, m) -> w_l, producing a witness that the seal l was closed over message m, and Verify(l, w_l, m) -> bool; practical implementations also add Gen(p) -> l to generate a new seal bound to a public key (or arbitrary predicate) and an authenticated Close(l, m, s) -> w_l. The security property is that it must be infeasible for an attacker to make Verify return true for two distinct messages m1 != m2 closed over the same seal (multiple witnesses for the same seal/message pair are tolerable but non-ideal). A trivial realisation is a trusted notary that signs witnesses; the scalable, trust-minimised realisation replaces the notary with a proof-of-publication ledger whose state is agreed in a trust-minimised way — i.e. the Bitcoin blockchain, where closing a seal corresponds to spending a specified transaction output and the commitment is published on-chain.
answer_key_points: Core ops: Close(l,m)->w and Verify(l,w,m)->bool; plus Gen(p)->l and authenticated Close(l,m,s)->w
A seal can be closed over a message exactly once
Security: infeasible to make Verify true for two distinct messages on the same seal
Multiple witnesses for the same seal/message pair are acceptable (non-ideal)
Trivial impl = trusted notary with disposable keys; trust-minimised = proof-of-publication ledger (Bitcoin)
On Bitcoin, closing a seal = spending the defined UTXO with an on-chain commitment

topic: RGB consignments and the transfer protocol
question: In RGB, data is moved between parties as 'consignments'. Distinguish a contract consignment from a transfer (terminal) consignment, explain why the two differ so much in size, and describe the role of the receiver's blinded UTXO and the 'stash' in a transfer.
reference_answer: A contract consignment is the small package needed to bootstrap a contract: it carries the contract Genesis plus its Schema (each on the order of a couple of hundred bytes, so the whole thing is typically a few KiB) and can be distributed by any channel — website, email, QR, Nostr, etc. A transfer (terminal) consignment is much larger because, in addition to the final state transition addressed to the recipient, it must include the entire validated history of state transitions back to Genesis so the receiver can independently verify the asset against the Bitcoin anchors. The receiver starts a transfer by issuing an invoice that encodes a seal definition — usually one of their UTXOs in blinded form — telling the sender where to assign the new owned state without revealing the exact outpoint. Each party keeps a 'stash' of client-side-validated data; the sender builds a PSBT/witness transaction embedding the Opret/Tapret DBC commitment (plus any 'blank' transitions for other assets on the same seal), generates the terminal consignment, and the receiver runs 'rgb accept' to validate it and merge it into their stash before the witness transaction is broadcast.
answer_key_points: Contract consignment = Genesis + Schema, only a few KiB
Transfer/terminal consignment = final state transition + full validated history since Genesis (hence much larger)
History is needed so the receiver can verify against Bitcoin anchors client-side
Invoice encodes a seal definition, typically the receiver's UTXO in blinded form
Stash = each party's store of client-side-validated data
Sender embeds Opret/Tapret DBC in a PSBT (plus blank transitions); receiver 'rgb accept' validates before broadcast

question: RGB separates a contract 'Schema' from a contract 'Interface'. Explain what each is, how an RGB Schema differs fundamentally from an Ethereum on-chain contract, and how RGB interfaces (e.g. RGB20, RGB21, RGB25) relate to the concrete schemas an issuer uses.
reference_answer: An RGB Schema is a declarative template — analogous to a class — that defines the kinds of owned state and assignments, the global state, the structure of Genesis, the permitted state transitions and their metadata, and, crucially, embeds the AluVM state-validation scripts that encode the business logic. It is compiled to a .rgb/.rgba binary and an issuer instantiates it by filling in values (ticker, name, precision, issued supply, initial allocations) in Genesis. This is fundamentally different from Ethereum, where the contract itself is executable bytecode whose state lives on-chain; in RGB the contract is purely declarative and validated client-side, with nothing but a commitment published on Bitcoin. Interfaces, introduced in v0.10, are the standardised APIs through which wallets read and act on a contract — comparable to Ethereum ABIs/ERCs — but, unlike ERCs, they need neither obligatory standardisation nor separate distribution because they travel bundled with the contract, and additional interfaces can be attached to an immutable contract over time. RGB20 is the fungible-asset interface (implemented by the NIA schema), RGB21 is for unique/collectible digital assets/NFTs (UDA), and RGB25 is for collectible fungible assets (CFA); the schema provides the implementation while the interface provides the semantic, wallet-facing view.
answer_key_points: Schema = declarative template (like a class): owned/global state, assignments, transitions, metadata, embedded AluVM validation scripts
Issuer instantiates a schema in Genesis (ticker, precision, issued supply, allocations); compiled to .rgb/.rgba
Unlike Ethereum, the RGB contract is declarative and validated client-side; only a commitment goes on Bitcoin
Interfaces (v0.10+) are ABI/ERC-like APIs but bundled with the contract, needing no separate standardisation/distribution
Multiple interfaces can be added to an immutable contract over time
RGB20 = fungible (NIA), RGB21 = unique/NFT (UDA), RGB25 = collectible fungible (CFA)

question: RGB's consensus data is represented with 'Strict Types' rather than a conventional serialization. What distinguishes strict types from algebraic data types in languages like Haskell, what is the 64 KiB rule, and why does RGB compile its whole consensus layer into strict types?
reference_answer: Strict types are a formal, deterministic notation for algebraic data types aimed at real computing/networking platforms rather than abstract theory. Their defining difference from Haskell/Idris-style ADTs is that every collection must carry explicit minimum and maximum bounds as part of the type itself, so resource requirements are known at compile time and runtime exceptions are avoided. They are deterministic (any two byte sequences that differ represent semantically distinct data) and impose a resource limit: no atomic encoded data piece may exceed 64 KiB, which lets even embedded/limited-memory devices process the data. Because the type system is formal, one can formally verify that (de)serialization matches a schema and prove statements about memory-layout equivalence and convertibility. RGB compiles its entire consensus layer into strict types so it can obtain compile-time size guarantees (helping hardware wallets) and, most importantly, produce formal proofs of binary compatibility between releases. Strict types were developed by Maxim Orlovsky under the UBIDECO Institute and are also used by AluVM and other client-side-validation systems.
answer_key_points: Formal, deterministic notation for ADTs targeting real platforms, not abstract theory
Every collection has explicit min/max bounds baked into the type -> compile-time resource prediction, no runtime exceptions
Determinism: differing byte sequences always mean semantically distinct data
64 KiB rule: no atomic encoded piece may exceed 64 KiB, enabling embedded/limited-memory use
Enables formal verification of (de)serialization and memory-layout equivalence
RGB compiles its whole consensus layer to strict types for binary-compatibility proofs across releases; by Orlovsky/UBIDECO

question: Bifrost (LNPBP-50, with LNPBP-51 and LNPBP-53) is proposed as a replacement/extension networking layer for Lightning, in part to carry RGB data. Why did the LNP/BP designers introduce a new protocol instead of extending the BOLTs, what encoding change is central to it, and what do LNPBP-51 and LNPBP-53 add on top of the LNPBP-50 core?
reference_answer: Bifrost was introduced because extending the BOLTs is painful: each atomic feature touches several separate standards, experimental features are hard to isolate from tested core code, and BOLT messaging was designed narrowly for payments — making non-payment state channels, messaging/DEX use and RGB data propagation awkward to bolt on. A central technical motivation is encoding: BOLTs use BigInt encoding, which is unsuitable for client-side-validated data, so Bifrost re-encodes all message fields with strict encoding. LNPBP-50 is the generalized networking core — it runs over TCP on a dedicated default port 9913, reuses Lightning's Noise_XK handshake/encryption and message framing (extracted as LNPBP-15/18), advertises support via a local-features flag, and defines bifrost:// URLs. On top of that core, LNPBP-51 specifies the channel-management protocol and LNPBP-53 specifies multi-peer payment channels for Bifrost (with further LNPBPs covering routed messaging, channel factories and HTLC/PTLC synchronization). Related standard LNPBP-35 defines the Bifrost message extensions used to propagate RGB data over Lightning.
answer_key_points: Extending BOLTs is hard: features span multiple standards, no isolation of experimental code, payment-only design
BigInt encoding in BOLTs is unsuitable for client-side-validated data -> Bifrost uses strict encoding for all fields
LNPBP-50 = generalized core: TCP, dedicated default port 9913, Noise_XK (LNPBP-15) + framing (LNPBP-18), bifrost:// URLs, local-features flag
LNPBP-51 = channel-management protocol
LNPBP-53 = multi-peer payment channels for Bifrost
LNPBP-35 (related) carries RGB data propagation over Lightning

question: Carbonado is the archival storage format associated with RGB wallet stash persistence (notably in BitMask). It is described as 'apocalypse-resistant data storage for the truly paranoid'. What combination of cryptographic and coding techniques does it layer into a single flat-file container, and what problem is each layer solving?
reference_answer: Carbonado is a single flat-file archival container designed for long-term, consensus-critical data such as an RGB stash, layering several independent techniques. It applies authenticated symmetric encryption (in the v2 format, AES-256-CTR with full HMAC-SHA512 encrypt-then-MAC) to provide confidentiality and integrity of the private client-side-validated data. It uses Bao — a BLAKE3-based tree hashing scheme — to give verified streaming with per-slice (4 KiB) verifiability, so any portion can be authenticated without reading the whole file. It adds Reed-Solomon forward error correction (a deterministic 4/8 scheme) so the archive survives bit-rot and partial media loss, and optional Zstandard compression to reduce size. Newer versions also attach post-quantum (SLH-DSA / FIPS-205) signatures as optional sidecars. Together these layers target the goal of data that stays private, verifiable and recoverable over very long horizons and degraded storage — matching RGB's model where losing your client-side history means losing the asset.
answer_key_points: Single flat-file archival container for long-term consensus-critical data (e.g. RGB stash), used by BitMask
Authenticated encryption (v2: AES-256-CTR + HMAC-SHA512 encrypt-then-MAC) for confidentiality + integrity
Bao (BLAKE3-based) verified streaming with per-4 KiB-slice verifiability
Reed-Solomon forward error correction (deterministic 4/8) against bit-rot / partial loss
Optional Zstandard compression; optional post-quantum SLH-DSA (FIPS-205) signature sidecars
Purpose: private, verifiable, recoverable data because losing client-side history loses the RGB asset

topic: did:nostr DID method (construction, resolution, verification relationships)
question: In the did:nostr DID method, what exactly is the method-specific identifier, and what does a resolver produce in the minimal (offline) resolution tier? Specifically, name the verification method type and the two verification relationships that must reference it, and describe how the publicKeyMultibase value is built from the Nostr key.
reference_answer: The method-specific identifier is the 64-character lowercase hexadecimal x-only secp256k1 public key (the same key material as an npub, but npub bech32 is display-only, never the DID id): a DID looks like did:nostr:<64-hex>. In the minimal, network-free tier a conformant resolver MUST deterministically derive a DID document from the key alone: id set to the full DID, type "DIDNostr", a single verification method of type "Multikey", and both authentication and assertionMethod referencing that method by a relative DID URL such as "#key1". The publicKeyMultibase is constructed as multibase base16-lower (prefix "f") over the secp256k1 compressed-key multicodec varint (0xe7 0x01) followed by the parity byte and the 32-byte x-only key. Optional HTTP resolution fetches https://<domain>/.well-known/did/nostr/<pubkey>.json, and optional "enhanced" resolution queries relays for kind 0 (profile), kind 3 (follows) and kind 10002 (relay list) to enrich the document — but there is no special "DID document" event kind.
answer_key_points: Method-specific id = 64-char lowercase hex x-only secp256k1 pubkey; npub is display-only
Minimal document is derived offline from the key alone, with type "DIDNostr"
Verification method type is "Multikey"; authentication and assertionMethod both reference #key1
publicKeyMultibase = 'f' (base16 multibase) + e701 (secp256k1 multicodec) + parity byte + hex key
Three-tier resolution: minimal (offline) -> HTTP .well-known/did/nostr/<pubkey>.json -> enhanced relay query (kind 0/3/10002); no dedicated DID-document event kind

question: How does NIP-05 map a name@domain identifier to a Nostr public key? Give the exact HTTP request a client makes, the structure of the JSON returned, the meaning of the special '_' name, and the core security rule about what a client must actually follow.
reference_answer: A NIP-05 identifier is the 'nip05' field on a user's kind 0 metadata event. To verify local-part@domain, the client issues a GET to https://<domain>/.well-known/nostr.json?name=<local-part> (local-part restricted to a-z0-9-_.). The response is a JSON object with a required 'names' object mapping each name to a lowercase hex public key, plus an optional 'relays' object keyed by hex pubkey giving arrays of relay URLs. The name '_' is a root identifier displayed as just the bare domain (so alice can be _@alice.com shown as 'alice.com'). Crucially, NIP-05 is only a human-friendly pointer, not an identity: clients MUST follow the public key, not the NIP-05 address — if the key behind an address changes, the client keeps the original pubkey and stops showing the now-invalid address. Servers MUST NOT return HTTP redirects and should send Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *.
answer_key_points: Request: GET https://<domain>/.well-known/nostr.json?name=<local-part>
JSON has required 'names' (name -> lowercase hex pubkey) and optional 'relays' (pubkey -> [relay URLs])
'_' is the root identifier, displayed as the bare domain name
Security rule: clients follow the pubkey, never the NIP-05 address as primary identity
No redirects allowed; CORS header Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * recommended

question: What is the NIP-07 window.nostr capability, and what problem does it solve for Nostr web apps? Name the two mandatory methods and their signatures, describe what signEvent receives and returns, and list the optional encryption namespaces.
reference_answer: NIP-07 defines a window.nostr object injected by a browser extension or signer so that a web app can request Nostr operations without ever handling the user's private key — the key stays inside the extension, and the page only ever sees signatures and the pubkey. The two mandatory methods are async window.nostr.getPublicKey(): string (returns the pubkey as hex) and async window.nostr.signEvent(event): Event. signEvent receives an unsigned event object { created_at, kind, tags, content } and returns the same event completed with the id, pubkey and sig fields filled in. Optional namespaces provide encryption: window.nostr.nip04.encrypt/decrypt(pubkey, ...) (now deprecated) and window.nostr.nip44.encrypt/decrypt(pubkey, ...). Extensions typically run at document_end so window.nostr is present when pages load.
answer_key_points: window.nostr is injected by an extension/signer so the private key never reaches the web page
getPublicKey(): returns hex pubkey
signEvent(event) takes {created_at, kind, tags, content} and returns it with id, pubkey, sig added
Optional nip04 (deprecated) and nip44 encrypt/decrypt namespaces
getRelays() optional; extension injected at document_end

question: NIP-19 defines both bare bech32 entities (npub, nsec, note) and TLV-carrying ones (nprofile, nevent, naddr). Which bech32 variant does it use, and what are the four TLV type numbers and their meanings? Explain concretely how an nprofile differs from an npub and what data an naddr must carry.
reference_answer: NIP-19 uses plain bech32 — explicitly bech32 'not-m', i.e. NOT bech32m — for all of these entities. Bare types (npub/nsec/note) are just the hex pubkey, seckey or event id re-encoded in bech32. The TLV types (nprofile/nevent/naddr, plus deprecated nrelay) pack multiple 1-byte-type / 1-byte-length / value records. The four TLV types are: 0 = special (the primary payload — a 32-byte pubkey for nprofile, a 32-byte event id for nevent, or the UTF-8 identifier 'd' string for naddr); 1 = relay (an ASCII relay URL, optional and repeatable); 2 = author (a 32-byte pubkey — required for naddr, optional for nevent); 3 = kind (a big-endian 32-bit unsigned integer). So an nprofile is an npub plus optional relay hints, telling clients where to find that person, whereas an npub is only the key. An naddr, which addresses a replaceable/addressable event, must carry the identifier (type 0), the author pubkey (type 2) and the kind (type 3), optionally with relay hints.
answer_key_points: Uses bech32, explicitly NOT bech32m
Bare npub/nsec/note are hex re-encoded; nprofile/nevent/naddr carry TLV
TLV type 0 = special (pubkey / event id / identifier string depending on prefix)
TLV type 1 = relay (ASCII URL, repeatable); type 2 = author (32-byte pubkey); type 3 = kind (32-bit big-endian)
nprofile = pubkey + relay hints (vs bare npub); naddr must carry identifier + author + kind

question: Describe the NIP-42 challenge-response authentication flow between a Nostr client and a relay. What event kind is used, which two tags must it contain, what does the relay validate, and how does a relay signal that a request needs authentication?
reference_answer: NIP-42 lets a relay authenticate a client. The relay initiates by sending an ["AUTH", <challenge-string>] message over the connection. The client replies with ["AUTH", <signed-event>] where the event is an ephemeral kind 22242 event (relays MUST NOT broadcast it) with created_at at the current time and at least two tags: a ["relay", "wss://..."] tag naming the target relay and a ["challenge", "..."] tag echoing the relay's challenge. The relay validates that the kind is 22242, that created_at is within a small window (~10 minutes) of now, that the challenge tag matches the challenge it issued, and that the relay tag matches its own URL. When an unauthenticated client attempts a restricted action, the relay signals it with an OK/CLOSED message prefixed 'auth-required: ' (and 'restricted: ' when the authenticated key still lacks permission).
answer_key_points: Relay sends ["AUTH", challenge]; client returns ["AUTH", signed event]
Event is ephemeral kind 22242, never broadcast
Required tags: ["relay", url] and ["challenge", string]
Relay checks kind=22242, created_at within ~10 min, challenge match, relay URL match
'auth-required: ' prefix signals need to authenticate; 'restricted: ' for insufficient permission

topic: NIP-65 relay list metadata and the outbox model
question: What is a NIP-65 relay list, and how does it enable the 'outbox' (gossip) model? Give the event kind, the tag used to list relays, the meaning of the read/write markers including an unmarked entry, and the rule for where a client should look to fetch a given user's posts versus their mentions.
reference_answer: NIP-65 defines kind 10002, a replaceable event whose 'r' tags advertise a user's preferred relays, e.g. ["r", "wss://relay.example", "write"]. The optional third element is a marker: 'read' means a relay where the user reads (expects to receive mentions), 'write' means a relay where the user publishes; if the marker is omitted the relay is BOTH read and write. This drives the outbox/gossip model: to fetch a user's own events you query their WRITE relays, and to reach a user (mention/reply) you post to their READ relays — so followers converge on the author's own declared relays instead of everyone piling onto a few big relays. Clients should keep the list small (roughly 2-4 relays per category) and propagate the kind 10002 event widely, including to well-known indexers, so others can discover it.
answer_key_points: kind 10002, replaceable, uses 'r' tags with relay URLs
Markers 'read' and 'write'; omitted marker means both
Fetch a user's posts from their WRITE relays; send mentions/replies to their READ relays
Underpins the outbox/gossip model (spread load onto authors' own relays)
Keep list small (~2-4 per category); propagate widely / to indexers

question: In Solid-OIDC, how is a user's WebID conveyed and how does a resource server avoid trusting a rogue OpenID Provider that issues tokens for arbitrary WebIDs? Also explain the two Solid-OIDC features that remove the need for pre-registered clients and for bearer tokens, and how a DPoP proof (RFC 9449) is bound to the access token.
reference_answer: Solid-OIDC builds on OpenID Connect Authorization Code + PKCE. The ID Token carries a 'webid' claim (the user's WebID URI) alongside 'azp' (authorized party / client) and an 'aud' that includes azp and the string 'solid'. To stop a malicious OP minting valid-looking tokens for someone else's WebID, the verifier performs WebID Provider Confirmation: it dereferences the WebID profile and checks the triple ?webid <http://www.w3.org/ns/solid/terms#oidcIssuer> ?iss, i.e. that the token's issuer is one the WebID owner actually authorised (RDF statement or Link header). Two features remove classic friction: dynamic client identity, where the OAuth Client ID is itself a dereferenceable Client ID Document (JSON-LD using the solid/oidc-context) listing redirect_uris etc., so no manual pre-registration is needed; and DPoP-bound tokens instead of bearer tokens. Per RFC 9449, the client sends a DPoP proof JWT in the 'DPoP' header — JOSE header typ='dpop+jwt', an asymmetric 'alg', and a 'jwk' public key — with payload claims jti, htm (method), htu (URI) and iat (plus 'ath', the SHA-256 of the access token, when a token is presented). The access token's 'cnf' claim then contains 'jkt' = the base64url SHA-256 JWK thumbprint of that public key, so the resource server accepts it only from the holder of the matching private key, defeating stolen-token replay.
answer_key_points: ID Token carries webid claim, plus azp and aud including azp and 'solid'
WebID Provider Confirmation checks solid:oidcIssuer triple (http://www.w3.org/ns/solid/terms#oidcIssuer) so issuer matches WebID-authorised OP
Client ID is a dereferenceable Client ID Document (JSON-LD), removing static registration
DPoP proof JWT (RFC 9449): header typ=dpop+jwt/alg/jwk, claims jti/htm/htu/iat (+ath with a token)
Access token cnf.jkt = base64url SHA-256 JWK thumbprint binds the token to the client's DPoP key, preventing bearer-style replay

topic: Web Access Control (WAC) vs Access Control Policy (ACP)
question: Contrast Solid's two authorization systems, WAC and ACP. For WAC, name the authorization modes, the difference between acl:accessTo and acl:default, and how public access is granted. For ACP, name the core resource and objects (ACR, policy, matcher) and the boolean combinators, and state the key conceptual capability ACP adds that WAC lacks.
reference_answer: Both are RDF-based, but they differ in expressiveness. WAC (namespace http://www.w3.org/ns/auth/acl#) is a classic ACL model: an acl:Authorization grants acl:mode values acl:Read, acl:Write, acl:Append and acl:Control (Control governs the ACL resource itself). acl:accessTo names the specific resource an authorization applies to, whereas acl:default is set on a container and is inherited by resources lower in the hierarchy that have no ACL of their own. Subjects are named with acl:agent (a specific agent), acl:agentGroup, or acl:agentClass — and public access is granted by using foaf:Agent as the agentClass (with acl:AuthenticatedAgent for any logged-in agent). The ACL resource is found via a Link header with rel="acl". ACP (namespace acp:) is attribute-/policy-based: an Access Control Resource (ACR) links a resource to acp:AccessControl objects that acp:apply acp:Policy objects; each Policy uses acp:allow/acp:deny access modes gated by acp:Matcher conditions combined with acp:allOf (AND), acp:anyOf (OR) and acp:noneOf (NOT). Crucially, matchers can test not just acp:agent but also acp:client (which application) and acp:issuer (which identity provider) and acp:vc (verifiable credentials) — contextual, attribute-based conditions WAC cannot express, since WAC decisions turn essentially on agent identity and mode alone.
answer_key_points: WAC modes: acl:Read, acl:Write, acl:Append, acl:Control (Control = over the ACL itself)
acl:accessTo = this resource; acl:default = on a container, inherited by contained resources lacking their own ACL
Public via acl:agentClass foaf:Agent; acl:AuthenticatedAgent = any logged-in agent; ACL found via Link rel=acl
ACP: ACR -> acp:AccessControl -> acp:Policy (acp:allow/acp:deny) gated by acp:Matcher via acp:allOf/anyOf/noneOf
ACP adds attribute/context conditions on acp:client, acp:issuer and acp:vc, not just agent identity

question: Explain how WebID-TLS authenticates an agent using a client certificate and the WebID profile document, naming the certificate field that carries the WebID and the RDF ontology terms a verifier matches the certificate key against. Then give the main reasons the Solid community moved from WebID-TLS to WebID-OIDC / Solid-OIDC.
reference_answer: In WebID-TLS the agent presents an X.509 client certificate whose Subject Alternative Name (SAN) is a dereferenceable URI — that URI is the WebID. The verification agent extracts the WebID from the SAN, dereferences the WebID profile (RDF, e.g. Turtle), and looks for public key material attached to that WebID via cert:key (namespace http://www.w3.org/ns/auth/cert#). For an RSA key the profile carries a cert:RSAPublicKey node with a cert:modulus (xsd:hexBinary) and a cert:exponent (xsd:integer, commonly 65537). The verifier compares the modulus/exponent in the certificate against those published in the profile; a match, combined with the TLS handshake proving possession of the private key, authenticates the agent as that WebID. The community moved to WebID-OIDC / Solid-OIDC mainly for usability and reach: browser client-certificate UX is poor (confusing certificate-selection dialogs, a Firefox restart quirk, no real 'log out', awkward multiple-identity handling, unsuitable on shared/public machines), client-cert support is weak on mobile and some browsers, and it is hard for non-browser clients. WebID-OIDC keeps the WebID concept but rides mainstream OAuth2/OIDC token flows (adding WebID Provider Confirmation), giving better UX, session/logout semantics and cross-platform support.
answer_key_points: WebID-TLS: WebID is carried in the certificate's SubjectAlternativeName (URI)
Verifier dereferences WebID profile and matches key via cert:key -> cert:RSAPublicKey with cert:modulus (hexBinary) and cert:exponent (integer)
TLS handshake proves private-key possession; key match binds cert to WebID
Moved away due to poor browser client-cert UX: confusing dialogs, no logout, multi-identity/shared-machine problems, weak mobile/browser support
Solid-OIDC keeps WebID but uses OAuth2/OIDC token flow plus WebID Provider Confirmation

question: In the Solid Notifications Protocol, how does a client subscribe to changes on a resource, and what are the two standard channel types? Give their exact type identifiers and namespace, the property used to name the resource of interest, and the response property that differs between the WebSocket and Webhook channels.
reference_answer: A client subscribes by sending an authenticated POST of a JSON-LD subscription request (context https://www.w3.org/ns/solid/notification/v1) to the subscription resource for a channel type. The request sets 'type' to the channel type and 'topic' (notify:topic) to the URL of the resource whose changes it wants. The two standard channel types live in the namespace http://www.w3.org/ns/solid/notifications# : WebSocketChannel2023 (notify:WebSocketChannel2023) and WebhookChannel2023 (notify:WebhookChannel2023). They differ in delivery direction: for a WebSocket subscription the server's response returns a receiveFrom (notify:receiveFrom) URL that the client opens a WebSocket to; for a Webhook subscription the client additionally supplies a sendTo (notify:sendTo) HTTPS URL in the request, and the server pushes notifications there (the response identifies the 'sender'). Notification payloads themselves are Activity Streams 2.0 objects serialized as JSON-LD.
answer_key_points: Subscribe via authenticated POST of JSON-LD (context .../solid/notification/v1) to the subscription resource
Channel types in namespace http://www.w3.org/ns/solid/notifications#
WebSocketChannel2023 and WebhookChannel2023
notify:topic names the target resource; WebSocket response gives notify:receiveFrom; Webhook request supplies notify:sendTo
Notifications are Activity Streams 2.0 JSON-LD

topic: OpenTimestamps Merkle aggregation, calendar servers and .ots proofs
question: How does OpenTimestamps let thousands of documents be timestamped by a single Bitcoin transaction, and what does a .ots proof actually contain? Describe the role of calendar servers, the two-step stamp-then-upgrade workflow, the kinds of operations and attestations inside a proof, and how verification recomputes the path to Bitcoin.
reference_answer: OpenTimestamps avoids one Bitcoin transaction per document by aggregation: clients send a document hash to public calendar servers, which insert it into a Merkle tree and periodically commit only the Merkle tree root into a single Bitcoin transaction (typically via an OP_RETURN output), so one transaction can anchor thousands of digests. The workflow is two-step. On 'stamp', the client hashes the file (SHA-256, with a random nonce for privacy) and receives an incomplete .ots receipt containing PendingAttestation(<calendar URL>) — it can't be verified yet because the Bitcoin transaction isn't confirmed. Later, 'upgrade' contacts the calendar and rewrites the .ots with the finished path and a BitcoinBlockHeaderAttestation, after which the proof is self-contained. A .ots proof is essentially a program: the file hash plus an ordered sequence of commitment operations (append <hex>, prepend <hex>, and hash ops such as sha256 / ripemd160) that walk from the document hash up through the Merkle tree and the Bitcoin transaction to a block's Merkle root, terminated by an attestation. Verification replays those operations starting from the document's own hash, reproduces the committed value, and checks it against the specified Bitcoin block header (needing only the file, the .ots proof and trusted block headers) — proving the document existed before that block was mined.
answer_key_points: Calendar servers aggregate many document hashes into a Merkle tree and commit only the root to Bitcoin via OP_RETURN (one tx anchors thousands)
Two steps: stamp yields an incomplete .ots with PendingAttestation(calendar URL); upgrade adds BitcoinBlockHeaderAttestation
.ots is an ordered path of operations: append/prepend <hex> and hash ops (sha256, ripemd160)
Verification replays ops from the document hash up to the Bitcoin block Merkle root / header
Completed proof is self-contained: needs only file + .ots + trusted Bitcoin block headers
